statement: In kinematics, angular velocity is a vector or pseudovector \boldsymbol{\omega} (or scalar \omega in two dimensions) representing the rate of rotation and the orientation of the instantaneous axis of rotation. For a point particle with position vector \mathbf{r} relative to a chosen origin and velocity \mathbf{v}, the orbital angular velocity in three dimensions is defined as \boldsymbol{\omega} = \frac{\mathbf{r} \times \mathbf{v}}{r^2} = \frac{v \sin(\theta)}{r} \mathbf{u} = \frac{d\phi}{dt} \mathbf{u}, where r = \|\mathbf{r}\|, \theta is the angle between \mathbf{r} and \mathbf{v}, and \mathbf{u} is the unit vector normal to the instantaneous plane of rotation specified by the right-hand rule. In two dimensions, orbital angular velocity is defined as \omega = \frac{d\phi}{dt} = \frac{v_\perp}{r}.

symbols.meaning: angular speed (magnitude of angular velocity vector)
unit vector normal to the instantaneous plane of rotation satisfying the right-hand rule
position vector of the particle from the origin
scalar distance to origin or orbital radius (r = \|\mathbf{r}\|)
angle between position vector \mathbf{r} and linear velocity vector \mathbf{v}
orthonormal basis unit vectors fixed in a rotating frame (i = 1, 2, 3)

properties.property: Tangential velocity is recovered from angular velocity via \mathbf{v}_\perp = \boldsymbol{\omega} \times \mathbf{r}
properties.why: cross-radial velocity is orthogonal to both the rotation axis and position vector with magnitude r\omega

properties.property: For a rigid body rotating about origin O with body-fixed orthonormal basis \mathbf{e}_1, \mathbf{e}_2, \mathbf{e}_3, spin angular velocity is \boldsymbol{\omega} = (\dot{\mathbf{e}}_1 \cdot \mathbf{e}_2)\mathbf{e}_3 + (\dot{\mathbf{e}}_2 \cdot \mathbf{e}_3)\mathbf{e}_1 + (\dot{\mathbf{e}}_3 \cdot \mathbf{e}_1)\mathbf{e}_2
properties.why: time derivatives of the body-fixed orthonormal vectors define the single instantaneous axis and rate of rotation common to all particles

properties.property: The velocity of any point \mathbf{r} in a rotating frame with fixed reference point \mathbf{r}_0 is \dot{\mathbf{r}} = \dot{\mathbf{r}}_0 + \boldsymbol{\omega} \times (\mathbf{r} - \mathbf{r}_0)
properties.why: all points in a rigid frame share a common instantaneous spin angular velocity about the rotation axis

properties.property: In circular motion of radius r, linear speed relates to angular speed by v = r\omega
properties.why: arc-length is \ell = r\phi, so differentiating with respect to time gives v = d\ell/dt = r(d\phi/dt) = r\omega

properties.property: Angular velocity behaves as a pseudoscalar in two dimensions and as a pseudovector in three dimensions
properties.why: parity inversion preserves magnitude but flips the sign or reverses axis orientation under the right-hand rule convention

properties.property: Angular velocity vectors of reference frames add commutatively: \boldsymbol{\omega}_1 + \boldsymbol{\omega}_2 = \boldsymbol{\omega}_2 + \boldsymbol{\omega}_1
properties.why: composition of linear movements defines standard vector addition for rotating frames

properties.property: Spin angular velocity decomposes along Euler angle axes as \boldsymbol{\omega} = \dot{\alpha}\mathbf{u}_1 + \dot{\beta}\mathbf{u}_2 + \dot{\gamma}\mathbf{u}_3
properties.why: projections of the angular velocity pseudovector onto precession, nutation, and intrinsic rotation axes equal the time derivatives of the corresponding Euler angles

assumptions.assumption: The particle's position vector in three dimensions is twice-continuously differentiable with respect to time
assumptions.breaks_when: The trajectory lacks required differentiability, leaving linear velocity or the center of curvature undefined

assumptions.assumption: The distance from the reference origin is non-zero (r = \|\mathbf{r}\| \neq 0)
assumptions.breaks_when: The particle is located at or passes through the origin, causing division by zero in \boldsymbol{\omega} = (\mathbf{r} \times \mathbf{v})/r^2

assumptions.assumption: The spatial dimension is exactly three for pseudovector characterization
assumptions.breaks_when: The motion takes place in spatial dimensions d > 3, where spin angular velocity cannot be represented as a vector and must instead be described by an antisymmetric rank-2 tensor

assumptions.assumption: The body or frame is rigid
assumptions.breaks_when: The body deforms or particles move relative to one another, preventing a single common spin angular velocity across all points

failure_modes.signature: Division by zero yielding undefined angular velocity
failure_modes.cause: Evaluating orbital angular velocity at r = 0 where the denominator r^2 vanishes

failure_modes.signature: Angular velocity vanishes (\boldsymbol{\omega} = \mathbf{0}) despite non-zero linear speed (v > 0)
failure_modes.cause: Linear velocity is parallel or antiparallel to the position vector (\mathbf{r} \times \mathbf{v} = \mathbf{0}), sweeping zero angle relative to the origin

failure_modes.mode: Application of single-particle formula to rigid bodies
failure_modes.signature: Varying angular velocity across points in a body instead of a single uniform rigid-body angular velocity
failure_modes.cause: Using the single-point orbital expression (\mathbf{r} \times \mathbf{v})/r^2, which is incompatible with rigid body motion where a single \boldsymbol{\omega} must account for all particles

failure_modes.signature: Vector cross product is undefined or fails to specify an axis of rotation
failure_modes.cause: Working in spatial dimensions greater than 3 where rotations occur in 2D planes without a unique normal vector axis
